subtopics.title: Iran-Israel Rivalry and the Axis of Resistance
subtopics.summary: Iran and Israel were allies during the Shah's reign, but relations turned hostile after the 1979 revolution, when the new Islamic government broke all ties with Israel. The Revolutionary Guard Corps then built a network of armed groups called the Axis of Resistance to confront Israel and its rivals. Its members include Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and Ansar Allah (Houthis) in Yemen.
facts: Iran and Israel were allies during the reign of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
The Shah was ousted in 1979 and an Islamic State was established in Iran.
The Khomeini government broke all relations with Israel after 1979.
The Shah ordered Khomeini to leave Iran in 1964; Khomeini then led the revolution from Iraq.
Khomeini called America the 'Big Devil' and Israel the 'Little Devil'.
The IRGC created the Axis of Resistance, a network of armed groups.
Hezbollah (Lebanon) was formed to fight Israeli forces that had invaded Lebanon in 1982.
Hamas (Gaza City) is linked to the outbreak of the First Intifada against Israel.
Ansar Allah emerged in Yemen as an opposition movement against President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Iran supports the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon as pressure fronts against Israel.

subtopics.title: Strait of Hormuz and Global Energy Shock
subtopics.summary: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is the only maritime outlet for the Gulf's oil and gas exports. The booklet warns that a blockade could push Brent crude prices up and possibly trigger a global energy crisis. Speculative demand from a risk premium can raise prices even before any supply is actually lost.
facts: The strait lies between Iran (north) and the Musandam Peninsula of Oman (south).
It connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and further to the Arabian Sea.
It is the only maritime outlet for the Persian Gulf's oil and gas exports.
It carries nearly 20% of global oil supply.
About 1/5 of global LNG trade and 1/3 of global fertiliser exports transit this corridor.
Traders add a risk premium, which can create artificial price rises through speculative demand.
Conflict could spill into the Red Sea or Suez Canal, raising transit times and freight costs.
India imports about 85% of its crude oil.
Each $1 rise in oil price adds about $1.5 billion a year to India's import bill.
Nearly 40% of India's crude oil imports and over 80% of its LPG imports pass through the strait.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Talks and Military Strikes
subtopics.summary: Nuclear talks in Geneva collapsed over US demands that Iran dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt uranium enrichment. The joint offensive then used heavy bombers, including US B-2 bunker-buster strikes on Fordow. Iran responded with missiles, including the Sejjil, in strikes on Israeli and US military bases.
facts: The 2015 JCPOA was signed between Iran and the P5+1 group of countries.
Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment to 3.67%.
The US withdrew from the JCPOA unilaterally in 2018 and reinstated sanctions.
Geneva talks collapsed over US demands to dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt enrichment.
US B-2 bombers used bunker-buster bombs to strike the fortified Fordow facility.
US airstrikes targeted Kharg Island, which handles nearly 90% of Iran's crude oil exports.
Iranian missiles struck near the heavily protected Dimona nuclear research centre.
The US B-1B Lancer, nicknamed 'Bone', was deployed in Operation Epic Fury.
The Sejjil is a two-stage, solid-fuel, medium-range ballistic missile.
The Sejjil is called the 'Dancing Missile' for its high-altitude manoeuvrability.

subtopics.title: Iran's Supreme Leader
subtopics.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei was named Iran's third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei was assassinated, the first hereditary-style transfer since the revolution. The office holds ultimate authority over Iran's political, military and religious institutions. The leader is chosen by the 88-member Assembly of Experts, and the office's authority derives from the doctrine of Velayat-e Faqih.
facts: Mojtaba Khamenei was named the third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei's assassination.
This was the first hereditary-style leadership transfer in Iran since the revolution.
The Supreme Leader is Iran's de jure head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
The office oversees national security and foreign policy and influences the election vetting process.
The Supreme Leader's authority derives from Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist).
Ruhollah Khomeini institutionalised this doctrine and was Iran's first Supreme Leader.
The Assembly of Experts is an 88-member clerical body elected by the public.
The Assembly of Experts elects the leader, supervises his performance and can remove him if unfit.
The 1989 constitutional amendment relaxed the earlier requirement that the leader be a Marja.

subtopics.title: India's Energy Security and Reserves
subtopics.summary: India imports about 85% of its crude oil, and a large share of its crude and LPG imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Its Strategic Petroleum Reserves are meant to cushion supply shocks, with current storage of about 3.37 MMT against a total capacity of 5.33 MMT. The government invoked the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 to ensure LPG availability during the crisis.
facts: India imports about 85% of its crude oil.
Nearly 40% of India's crude oil imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
More than 80% of India's LPG imports also transit the same route.
Qatar supplies nearly half of India's LNG imports.
Global crude oil prices have risen by about $20 per barrel (about 30%).
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserve has a total capacity of 5.33 million tonnes, with about 3.37 MMT in storage.
The Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited manages the SPR under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The global norm is to maintain 90 days of net oil import reserves.
The Essential Commodities Act, 1955 was invoked to ensure LPG availability.
West Asia accounts for 60-70% of India's basmati rice exports.

quizzes.title: Iran-Israel Rivalry: Background
quizzes.passage:
Relations between Iran and Israel have passed through sharply different phases. During the reign of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the two countries were allies, and their ties continued for years. This changed with the 1979 revolution, when the Shah was ousted and an Islamic State was established in Iran. The new government broke all relations with Israel and treated it as an enemy. Ruhollah Khomeini, the religious leader behind the revolution, had earlier been a fierce critic of the Shah and had been forced out of Iran. From exile in Iraq, he continued to lead the revolutionary movement, and he developed a strongly anti-Western and anti-Israeli outlook.

The rivalry was not limited to diplomacy. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps built a wider network of armed groups across West Asia. The network was meant to confront Israel, the United States and other rival powers in the region. Its members included organisations in Lebanon, Gaza and Yemen. Each group had its own origin, leadership and political character, yet together they created pressure fronts against Israel. This proxy strategy became one of the main sources of tension in the region and remains central to understanding the present conflict.

quizzes.title: Hormuz and India's Energy Exposure
quizzes.passage:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway that connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and, beyond it, to the Arabian Sea. It is the only maritime outlet for the oil and gas exports of the Persian Gulf, which makes it one of the most critical energy chokepoints in the world. Because so much energy passes through it, any threat to shipping in the strait is watched closely by markets. Traders often add a risk premium when disruption seems possible, and this speculative demand can push prices up before any actual supply is lost. If the conflict spreads to the Red Sea or the Suez Canal, shipping routes would be affected, transit times would increase and freight costs would rise. Supply bottlenecks could follow.

For a large importer like India, such shocks reach the economy in several ways. Higher crude prices widen the import bill, add pressure on the rupee and feed into inflation in transport, fertilisers and manufacturing. The government may absorb part of the shock through excise duty cuts, which can worsen the fiscal deficit. Fuel subsidies for LPG and urea may also rise. Energy-intensive industries face higher input costs and shrinking margins, while a wider current account deficit adds to the strain on the economy.
